The equality is unchanged by the exact coordinate transformations because all Jacobian and normalization factors remain inside the same normalized integral once. Every entry of the finite matrix converges along the common subsequence, so the closed positive-semidefinite cone contains the limiting matrix. This proves the claim. Yang–Mills Existence, Mass Gap, and Nontriviality for Fixed Compact Simple Gauge Groups via Karcher Blocking and Exact Haar–Pivot Matching Harold D. Kirk III1,2,∗ 1 University of Memphis, Memphis, Tennessee 38152, USA 2 ORCID: 0009-0000-6014-8451 August 3, 2026 Abstract Let G be a fixed compact connected simple Lie group and let ρ be a fixed faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation. We construct four-dimensional pure G Yang–Mills theory as a zero-spacing, infinite-volume limit of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures. The Wilson plaquette function is normalized at the identity to the background quadratic form used to define the coupling u = g2 . A weighted forty-nine-path Karcher block, complete sixteen-alias normal section, charged chart- complement partition, and permanent rooted domain produce a uniform scale-two map on a centered invariant graph, u(2L) = u(L) + 11 CA(G) log 2 24π2 u(L)2 + OG(u(L)3 ). The complete linear block certificate is independent of color and tensors with Ig; all nonlinear constants are finite and may depend on G. At the physical handoff, a group-dependent product Sobolev order 2sG > dG/2 gives a Peter–Weyl Fourier–Wiener landing for the exact one-pivot and multipivot densities. Separated Haar pivots contract nonvacuum compact flux, optical covariance contracts normal-field stretches, and all remaining vertices retain their support charge. A single marked replica–BKAR forest then gives a boundary-to-center two-root connector and one physical clustering rate. General invariant-jet transport, displacement and stress Ward identities, finite dimension-four mixing, and a dimension-six rotation regulator yield a tempered, reflection-positive, translation-continuous, O(4)-covariant Schwinger family. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction gives a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with unique vacuum and a strictly positive Hamiltonian gap. Endpoint-safe curvature-source transport produces a nonzero local vector with positive spectral mass in a finite interval above the gap. The theorem concerns the local gauge-invariant curvature-jet observable theory. The physical scale, thermodynamic limit, zero lattice spacing, Euclidean covariance, local spectral content, and non-abelian field geometry must be controlled in one compatible construction. Fix throughout a compact connected simple Lie group G, a faithful unitary representation ρ : G → U(Vρ) of dimension dρ, and a positive normalization of the invariant quadratic form for which the adjoint color factor is denoted CA(G). The Wilson plaquette function is wG,ρ(U) = cρ  1 − 1 dρ Re Tr ρ(U)  , where cρ > 0 is chosen once so that the Hessian at the identity is the quadratic form used by the background-field coupling coordinate u = g2 . This choice is a finite linear normalization of the bare Wilson coupling and is part of the fixed-group input register. Theorem 1.1 (Four-dimensional Yang–Mills construction for fixed compact simple G). For every fixed pair (G, ρ) as above, there is a directed sequence of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures, with microscopic spacing tending to zero and periodic volume tending to infinity, whose local gauge-invariant curvature-jet Schwinger functions converge to a nontrivial Euclidean field theory on R4 . The limiting Schwinger family is tempered, permutation symmetric, reflection positive, translation continuous, exponentially clustering, and O(4) covariant. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction yields a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with a unique vacuum and a number m⋆(G) > 0 such that H Ω⊥ ≥ m⋆(G). On the centered invariant weak trajectory, the exact scale-two coupling map is u(2L) = u(L) + 11 CA(G) log 2 24π2 u(L)2 + OG(u(L)3 ), with uniform volume and cutoff control in the permanent weak regime. The reconstructed theory contains a nonzero reflected local curvature vector and positive spectral mass in a finite interval [m⋆(G), M⋆(G)]. 1.2 Fixed-group conventions and finite register Write g = Lie(G) and dG = dim G. All Haar measures are normalized. The finite-volume approximants use the ordinary periodic link space GE(Λ) with periodic gauge transformations; no twisted boundary condition or nontrivial finite-volume bundle sector is summed. This is sufficient for the claimed local theory on the contractible space R4 . The bi-invariant metric, exponential coordinates, Laplacian ∆G, Casimir eigenvalues, and operator norms are those determined by the declared quadratic form. In curvature formulas, Tr(XY ) denotes this normalized invariant bilinear pairing; raw representation traces are written Tr ρ(·). Let sG :=  dG 4  + 1, 2sG > dG 2 . The fixed-group constant register CG consists of the finite quantities used below: the injectivity and convexity radii, a positive local Karcher radius, finite holomorphic BCH and logarithm bounds through order 2sG + 3, the faithful-action Hessian and complement charge, the Peter–Weyl constant, the finite ordinary-periodic toron/seam template register, the adjoint color factor, and the finite invariant-jet dimensions through the retained degree. Every statement called uniform is uniform in cutoff, volume, directed depth, periodic wrapping, admitted exterior histories, and the finite reflected template family, but its constants may depend on CG. Proposition 1.2 (Reflection-positive Wilson input). For every finite periodic lattice Λ and u > 0, in the ordinary periodic link sector, dµG,ρ Λ,u(U) = Z−1 Λ,u exp " −u−1 X p wG,ρ(Up) # Y e dmG(Ue) is gauge invariant and reflection positive for coordinate reflections. Moreover wG,ρ ≥ 0, its zero set is the identity, and on one fixed identity neighborhood cG∥X∥2 ≤ wG,ρ(eX ) ≤ CG∥X∥2 . 3 Proof. The normalized character satisfies Re Tr ρ(U) ≤ dρ, with equality only when ρ(U) = I; faithfulness gives U = e. The Hessian statement follows from the chosen normalization and compactness. Up to a field- independent constant, each plaquette factor is exp{t(χρ +χρ)} with t > 0. Its power series is a nonnegative linear combination of characters of tensor products of ρ and ρ̄, and their irreducible decompositions have nonnegative integer multiplicities. The standard character-expansion reflection-positivity argument therefore applies. 1.3 Proof architecture The proof has four stages. First, the exact Karcher block is placed in a complete full-alias normal chart and combined with a charged chart-complement partition, permanent analytic domain, marked connected logarithm, Wick-stable jet block, and centered invariant graph. The folded spacetime symbol tensors with Ig, while all nonlinear estimates are admitted by the finite register CG. Second, exact background-scheme conjugacy identifies the universal marginal coefficient and a directed schedule reaches the compact matching scale. The higher product Sobolev operator Q p(1−∆p)sG replaces the rank-one order and supplies the fixed-G Fourier–Wiener rows. Third, complete Haar and optical variables are kept in one partition function. A mixed replica– BKAR forest makes every root-to-root path pay separated Haar contraction, optical covariance decay, or pre-existing support charge. Ordinary-periodic toron backgrounds, seams, reflections, and wrapping certificates enter only through the finite template theorem of Appendix D. Finally, a least-label source forest transports the complete invariant-jet system. The degree-four block is group-independent because a compact simple Lie algebra has a unique invariant symmetric bilinear form; possible cubic color tensors first enter the finite dimension-six block. Ward identities, rotation-defect estimates, reflection-positive recombination, and Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction give covariance, the unique vacuum, the gap, and noncollapse. 1.4 External inputs and exact proof boundary Only the theorem-level inputs in Table 1 are imported. The fixed-group geometry, action charge, higher Sobolev landing, periodic-toron template theorem, invariant-jet admission, matching constants, and noncollapse source are internal. It is not a logical input to Theorem 1.1: every common analytic theorem used here is stated and proved in this paper, and every new fixed-group admission is printed below. Appendix F gives a theorem-level specialization map so that a referee can identify which arguments are color-free, which tensor with Ig, and which require new group data. 1.6 Scope The theorem concerns the local gauge-invariant curvature-jet observable sector for each fixed compact connected simple G. It does not assert a bound uniform over groups, a simultaneous large-rank limit, control of every extended Wilson-line or generalized-symmetry sector, or uniqueness of the continuum limit outside the directed construction. Quotient groups are included through their actual compact link group. The construction uses only the ordinary periodic finite-volume sector and retains all flat toron backgrounds occurring in that sector; no claim about a sum over twisted boundary conditions is made or needed. 2 Fixed-group Wilson geometry and Karcher blocking Let Λ be a finite periodic four-dimensional lattice and use the reflection-positive Wilson measure of Proposition 1.2. For each oriented retained link, use the straight two-link path with weight 7/8 and the forty-eight signed-corner staples with weight 1/384 each. On a fixed strongly convex identity tube, define the retained link as their weighted Karcher mean in the bi-invariant metric. Lemma 2.1 (Fixed-group convex Karcher and holomorphic atlas). There are radii 0 < r0,G < r1,G such that the squared-distance functions, product, inverse, exponential, logarithm, and weighted Karcher critical point extend holomorphically to the corresponding local complexification tube. The Karcher Hessian is bounded below there by a positive constant depending only on G. All derivatives through arbitrary prescribed finite order are bounded on the smaller tube. Proof. A compact Lie group with a bi-invariant analytic metric has positive injectivity and strong-convexity radii. The sectional curvature is bounded because G is compact, and the Hessian comparison theorem gives a positive lower Hessian bound on a sufficiently small ball. In a faithful matrix representation the local complexification is an open neighborhood in the complexified group; multiplication, inversion, exponential, and the principal logarithm are holomorphic there. The analytic implicit-function theorem applied to the Karcher critical equation gives the holomorphic mean. Cauchy estimates on nested compact tubes give every fixed derivative order; standard compact Lie-group analytic facts are summarized in [15]. Proposition 2.2 (Exact block covariance and local submersion). The retained map is gauge covariant, orientation covariant, signed-hypercubic covariant, and aligned-reflection covariant. Its linearization at the flat connection has full retained rank. On one fixed weak tube it admits a finite-volume analytic normal section whose matrix kernel and first three marked derivatives are exponentially local, uniformly in volume. Proof. Every path has the same endpoints, and the weighted squared-distance functional is invariant under simultaneous left and right multiplication. Yang–Mills Existence, Mass Gap, and Nontriviality for Fixed Compact Simple Gauge Groups via Karcher Blocking and Exact Haar–Pivot Matching Harold D. Kirk III1,2,∗ 1 University of Memphis, Memphis, Tennessee 38152, USA 2 ORCID: 0009-0000-6014-8451 August 3, 2026 Abstract Let G be a fixed compact connected simple Lie group and let ρ be a fixed faithful finite-dimensional unitary representation. We construct four-dimensional pure G Yang–Mills theory as a zero-spacing, infinite-volume limit of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures. The Wilson plaquette function is normalized at the identity to the background quadratic form used to define the coupling u = g2 . A weighted forty-nine-path Karcher block, complete sixteen-alias normal section, charged chart- complement partition, and permanent rooted domain produce a uniform scale-two map on a centered invariant graph, u(2L) = u(L) + 11 CA(G) log 2 24π2 u(L)2 + OG(u(L)3 ). The complete linear block certificate is independent of color and tensors with Ig; all nonlinear constants are finite and may depend on G. At the physical handoff, a group-dependent product Sobolev order 2sG > dG/2 gives a Peter–Weyl Fourier–Wiener landing for the exact one-pivot and multipivot densities. Separated Haar pivots contract nonvacuum compact flux, optical covariance contracts normal-field stretches, and all remaining vertices retain their support charge. A single marked replica–BKAR forest then gives a boundary-to-center two-root connector and one physical clustering rate. General invariant-jet transport, displacement and stress Ward identities, finite dimension-four mixing, and a dimension-six rotation regulator yield a tempered, reflection-positive, translation-continuous, O(4)-covariant Schwinger family. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction gives a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with unique vacuum and a strictly positive Hamiltonian gap. Endpoint-safe curvature-source transport produces a nonzero local vector with positive spectral mass in a finite interval above the gap. The theorem concerns the local gauge-invariant curvature-jet observable theory. No estimate is asserted uniformly over the class of compact simple groups. ∗hkirk@memphis.edu 1 Contents 1 The compact-simple-group theorem and proof boundary 3 2 Fixed-group Wilson geometry and Karcher blocking 5 3 Charged chart complement and irregular sector 10 4 Permanent weak renormalization group 23 5 Invariant graph and universal coefficient 39 6 Directed handoff and higher-order Peter–Weyl landing 52 7 Compact boundary-to-center closure 71 8 General invariant jets and Ward identities 72 9 Continuum reconstruction and spectral gap 89 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 90 11 Completion for arbitrary fixed compact simple gauge groups 94 A Endpoint packet-shell verification 94 B Root data and representation normalization 109 C The fixed-group Sobolev and Peter–Weyl ledger 110 D Ordinary periodic torons, seams, and wrapping templates 110 E Invariant tensor spaces through engineering dimension six 111 F Theorem-level specialization and dependency map 112 G Representative fixed-group certifications 113 2 1 The compact-simple-group theorem and proof boundary 1.1 Problem and result The constructive Yang–Mills problem asks for a nontrivial quantum gauge field theory on R4 satisfying the Osterwalder–Schrader and Wightman requirements and possessing a strictly positive mass gap [1]. The physical scale, thermodynamic limit, zero lattice spacing, Euclidean covariance, local spectral content, and non-abelian field geometry must be controlled in one compatible construction. Fix throughout a compact connected simple Lie group G, a faithful unitary representation ρ : G → U(Vρ) of dimension dρ, and a positive normalization of the invariant quadratic form for which the adjoint color factor is denoted CA(G). The Wilson plaquette function is wG,ρ(U) = cρ  1 − 1 dρ Re Tr ρ(U)  , where cρ > 0 is chosen once so that the Hessian at the identity is the quadratic form used by the background-field coupling coordinate u = g2 . This choice is a finite linear normalization of the bare Wilson coupling and is part of the fixed-group input register. Theorem 1.1 (Four-dimensional Yang–Mills construction for fixed compact simple G). For every fixed pair (G, ρ) as above, there is a directed sequence of reflection-positive Wilson lattice measures, with microscopic spacing tending to zero and periodic volume tending to infinity, whose local gauge-invariant curvature-jet Schwinger functions converge to a nontrivial Euclidean field theory on R4 . The limiting Schwinger family is tempered, permutation symmetric, reflection positive, translation continuous, exponentially clustering, and O(4) covariant. Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction yields a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant local theory with a unique vacuum and a number m⋆(G) > 0 such that H Ω⊥ ≥ m⋆(G). On the centered invariant weak trajectory, the exact scale-two coupling map is u(2L) = u(L) + 11 CA(G) log 2 24π2 u(L)2 + OG(u(L)3 ), with uniform volume and cutoff control in the permanent weak regime. The reconstructed theory contains a nonzero reflected local curvature vector and positive spectral mass in a finite interval [m⋆(G), M⋆(G)]. 1.2 Fixed-group conventions and finite register Write g = Lie(G) and dG = dim G. All Haar measures are normalized. The finite-volume approximants use the ordinary periodic link space GE(Λ) with periodic gauge transformations; no twisted boundary condition or nontrivial finite-volume bundle sector is summed. This is sufficient for the claimed local theory on the contractible space R4 . The bi-invariant metric, exponential coordinates, Laplacian ∆G, Casimir eigenvalues, and operator norms are those determined by the declared quadratic form. In curvature formulas, Tr(XY ) denotes this normalized invariant bilinear pairing; raw representation traces are written Tr ρ(·). Let sG :=  dG 4  + 1, 2sG > dG 2 . The fixed-group constant register CG consists of the finite quantities used below: the injectivity and convexity radii, a positive local Karcher radius, finite holomorphic BCH and logarithm bounds through order 2sG + 3, the faithful-action Hessian and complement charge, the Peter–Weyl constant, the finite ordinary-periodic toron/seam template register, the adjoint color factor, and the finite invariant-jet dimensions through the retained degree. Every statement called uniform is uniform in cutoff, volume, directed depth, periodic wrapping, admitted exterior histories, and the finite reflected template family, but its constants may depend on CG. Proposition 1.2 (Reflection-positive Wilson input). For every finite periodic lattice Λ and u > 0, in the ordinary periodic link sector, dµG,ρ Λ,u(U) = Z−1 Λ,u exp " −u−1 X p wG,ρ(Up) # Y e dmG(Ue) is gauge invariant and reflection positive for coordinate reflections. The normalized character satisfies Re Tr ρ(U) ≤ dρ, with equality only when ρ(U) = I; faithfulness gives U = e. The Hessian statement follows from the chosen normalization and compactness. Up to a field- independent constant, each plaquette factor is exp{t(χρ +χρ)} with t > 0. Its power series is a nonnegative linear combination of characters of tensor products of ρ and ρ̄, and their irreducible decompositions have nonnegative integer multiplicities. The standard character-expansion reflection-positivity argument therefore applies. 1.3 Proof architecture The proof has four stages. First, the exact Karcher block is placed in a complete full-alias normal chart and combined with a charged chart-complement partition, permanent analytic domain, marked connected logarithm, Wick-stable jet block, and centered invariant graph. The folded spacetime symbol tensors with Ig, while all nonlinear estimates are admitted by the finite register CG. Second, exact background-scheme conjugacy identifies the universal marginal coefficient and a directed schedule reaches the compact matching scale. The higher product Sobolev operator Q p(1−∆p)sG replaces the rank-one order and supplies the fixed-G Fourier–Wiener rows. Third, complete Haar and optical variables are kept in one partition function. A mixed replica– BKAR forest makes every root-to-root path pay separated Haar contraction, optical covariance decay, or pre-existing support charge. Ordinary-periodic toron backgrounds, seams, reflections, and wrapping certificates enter only through the finite template theorem of Appendix D. Finally, a least-label source forest transports the complete invariant-jet system. The degree-four block is group-independent because a compact simple Lie algebra has a unique invariant symmetric bilinear form; possible cubic color tensors first enter the finite dimension-six block. Ward identities, rotation-defect estimates, reflection-positive recombination, and Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction give covariance, the unique vacuum, the gap, and noncollapse. 1.4 External inputs and exact proof boundary Only the theorem-level inputs in Table 1 are imported. The fixed-group geometry, action charge, higher Sobolev landing, periodic-toron template theorem, invariant-jet admission, matching constants, and noncollapse source are internal. Appendix F gives a theorem-level specialization map so that a referee can identify which arguments are color-free, which tensor with Ig, and which require new group data. 1.6 Scope The theorem concerns the local gauge-invariant curvature-jet observable sector for each fixed compact connected simple G. It does not assert a bound uniform over groups, a simultaneous large-rank limit, control of every extended Wilson-line or generalized-symmetry sector, or uniqueness of the continuum limit outside the directed construction. Quotient groups are included through their actual compact link group. The construction uses only the ordinary periodic finite-volume sector and retains all flat toron backgrounds occurring in that sector; no claim about a sum over twisted boundary conditions is made or needed. 2 Fixed-group Wilson geometry and Karcher blocking Let Λ be a finite periodic four-dimensional lattice and use the reflection-positive Wilson measure of Proposition 1.2. D Ordinary periodic torons, seams, and wrapping templates The finite-volume model used throughout is the ordinary periodic product space GE(Λ) with periodic gauge transformations. It is a single, explicit lattice model; no twisted boundary condition and no sum over nontrivial principal-bundle sectors is part of the construction. Since the target spacetime R4 is contractible, this restriction is compatible with the theorem’s local continuum scope. Define the compact set of ordinary periodic flat holonomies TG := {(h1, h2, h3, h4) ∈ G4 : [hµ, hν] = e for all µ, ν}. Lemma D.1 (Tree-gauge reduction of ordinary periodic flat fields). Every flat configuration in the ordinary periodic link model is gauge equivalent to a seam representative whose interior links are the identity and whose four fundamental seam holonomies form an element of TG. Conversely every element of TG defines such a flat periodic configuration. The remaining gauge action is simultaneous conjugation of the four holonomies. 110 Proof. Choose a maximal lattice tree in a fundamental periodic cell and gauge its links to the identity. Flatness makes the holonomy of a path depend only on its homotopy class. The four links closing the fundamental cycles therefore supply holonomies hµ. The commutator loop of two fundamental cycles is a product of plaquette boundaries, so flatness gives [hµ, hν] = e. Reversing this construction gives a flat seam representative from every commuting four-tuple. A gauge transformation at the tree root conjugates all four holonomies simultaneously, and all other gauge freedom has already been fixed. Lemma D.2 (Finite toron and seam atlas). For every fixed compact G, the set TG has a finite cover by ambient product-coordinate neighborhoods on which every block word, Karcher word, coarea factor, Haar factor, reflected word, and source word used in the proof is analytic in the local variables and in the toron parameters. All derivatives through order 2sG + 3 have a finite common bound. The aligned coordinate reflections and seam placements add only a finite template family. Proof. The commutator equations define a closed subset of compact G4 , hence TG is compact. Around each of its points choose ordinary product charts in the ambient manifold G4 ; no quotient chart or classification of singular conjugacy classes is required. In tree gauge, every local factor is a fixed finite composition of multiplication, inversion, the local exponential/logarithm, and the Karcher implicit function, with some arguments left- or right-multiplied by the fixed seam holonomies. These maps are analytic on a sufficiently small product neighborhood and have finite Cauchy bounds through the declared order. Compactness gives a finite subcover. There are four seam directions and a finite aligned-reflection family, so taking a finite maximum gives the common constants. Theorem D.3 (Ordinary-periodic toron and optical admission). The complete full-alias right-inverse, normal-section, optical-coercivity, Haar-minorization, owner, and boundary-to-center estimates hold uniformly over every flat toron background in TG, every admitted seam and aligned-reflection template, and every periodic wrapping certificate. The acoustic toron/background variables remain explicit and are never inverted. No constant uniform over different groups is asserted. Proof. Lift a seam representative to the universal covering lattice. A flat background is gauged to the identity there; deck translation in direction µ acts on Lie-algebra fields by the unitary operator Ad(hµ). Since the hµ commute, these unitary operators are simultaneously diagonalizable over the complexified color space. On each joint color eigenspace the folded block and optical symbols are therefore the identity-background, color-free symbols evaluated at a real quasi-momentum shifted by the corresponding deck phase. The estimates Af (k)Af (k)∗ ⪰ 49 2 I4, ∥P0(k)∥2 ≤ 8 49 , and the printed complex-strip and optical lower bounds hold for every real quasi-momentum. They consequently survive every toron phase without a loss of constant. The retained acoustic variables, including toron tangents, are kept in the exterior/background register; only the same normal optical complement is inverted. Lemma D.2 supplies the nonlinear, coarea, Haar, and marked derivative bounds uniformly over a finite toron/seam cover. On the covering lattice the local gauge trivialization sends every plaquette holonomy to a conjugate of the corresponding fluctuation plaquette. The representation-normalized Wilson function is conjugation invariant, so the charge and its differentiated finite-word ledger are unchanged by this trivialization. The 2sG differentiated bad-core row of Theorem 3.20 is therefore uniform on the same cover. Consequently the complete one-pivot score and Haar minorization retain their printed constants after taking the finite template maximum. On intersections use the fixed least-label owner, so no factor is duplicated. A wrapping certificate records only the four lattice directions, the fixed block range, a finite seam crossing pattern, and an aligned reflection type; there are finitely many such local templates at one normalized step. Their iteration is already controlled by the permanent wrapping ideal rather than by a sum over topological sectors. Taking the finite maximum proves the stated admission and leaves the joint Haar–optical boundary-to-center mechanism unchanged. The antisymmetric structure 111 tensor is always present through the bracket but contributes only inside the already retained covariant derivative and commutator jets. The manuscript uses the complete finite quotient generated by curvature, covariant derivatives, metric and epsilon contractions, invariant color tensors, total-difference classes, and equation-of-motion contacts through the declared engineering cutoff. Use the faithful seven-dimensional real fundamental representation, viewed unitarily after complexi- fication: wG,ρ(U) = cρ  1 − 1 7 Re Tr ρ(U)  . Then dG = 14, CA(G) = 4, sG = 4, and 2sG = 8 > 7. There is no primitive cubic invariant and the coefficient is 11 log 2/(6π2 ). Faithfulness again makes the identity the unique zero of the charge. For all three examples, the compact ordinary-periodic toron set TG ⊂ G4 is covered by Lemma D.2; Theorem D.3 then supplies the same color-free full-alias and optical constants. The spectral sum in Appendix C converges at the displayed orders, while all nonlinear constants remain finite and group dependent. These are concrete admissions, not hypotheses of the main theorem. A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Fix an engineering cutoff D. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF, hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). The maps include the regular/irregular partition of unity before the logarithm is taken, so no all-good denominator occurs. Write Wm(J) = log Zm(J) − log Zm(0) for the normalized finite-volume source logarithm. Iterating the exact maps Rm, . . . , Rjw and then the finite macrobridge is an identity, not an asymptotic expansion. A scale-labelled source forest is generated recursively as follows. A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Terms transported without joining retain their existing components. At the terminal matching logarithm, the remaining components are joined by the matching-scale connected cumulants. The ordering of children is fixed by the least source label, so isomorphic terms are not counted more than once. Lemma 8.6 (Exact multiscale Faà di Bruno forest formula). For every finite depth m and every fixed derivative order n, Dn Wm(0)[J1, . . . , Jn] = X τ∈Tm,n Am(τ; J1, . . . , Jn), (115) where Tm,n is the finite family of recursively generated scale-labelled connected trees described above. Each analytic coefficient of each exact conditional logarithm occurs exactly once. After absolute values are taken, the sum is dominated uniformly in m by the rooted weak rows and the finite matching expansion. Hence (115) passes to the infinite weak-depth limit termwise for every fixed n. Proof. For one conditional integration, differentiation of the normalized logarithm is the joint-cumulant identity. The set-partition formula for a derivative of a composition is precisely the Banach-valued Faà di Bruno formula: every block of the partition is one incoming connected component and the outer cumulant joins those blocks at the current scale. Fixing the least-label order makes this representation unique. Induction over the finite sequence of exact conditional integrations proves (115); the terminal matching logarithm is the final induction step. The weak rooted margin pays every nonroot weak vertex by σ < 1, while the finite macrobridge and matching KP expansion pay the finitely many terminal vertices. The one/two-root bounds control a component while its source leaves remain external. These majorants are summable independently of m, so dominated convergence gives the last assertion. For a tree carrying two distinguished source buffers, let v(A, B) be their unique lowest common ancestor. If v(A, B) belongs to the terminal matching logarithm, call the history a matching history. Otherwise its scale label j(v) is the unique weak coarsest-connection scale. Notice that this is a property of the exact recursively generated tree, not a choice made after absolute values or bounds have been applied. Corollary 8.7 (No omission and no double counting). Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(FµαFνα), δµν Tr F2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. Uniqueness of the lowest common ancestor is the ordinary tree property. Lemma A.12 (Top marked ancestor and complete-packet shell). In a packet tree from Lemma A.11, contract every maximal descendant subtree carrying no distinguished label into its exact parent-normalized decoration, and suppress every maximal unary chain into its exact ordered transfer product. The distin- guished labels are the two curvature roots and the zero, one or two active g marks. They have a unique lowest common ancestor v⊤; let j be its conditional scale. Call v⊤ the top marked ancestor. All vertices strictly above v⊤ are unmarked. The complete coefficient created at v⊤ includes every contracted side decoration with its canonical reported support. Decompose these whole coefficients by their full reported-support shell k using a scalar translation- and reflection-invariant selector. The selected class is therefore a complete BRS/reflection packet with every denominator and normalization contact still inside it. If j ≤ k + C0, the permanent rooted-support row of that whole packet gives C(1 + 2k−j )q e−c2k−j . (208) If j > k + C0, the full support lies inside a fixed enlargement of one scale-j cell and no spatial connector estimate is needed. Proof. Contraction of an unlabelled descendant is its exact conditional value, so it retains its canonical reported support. Suppression of a unary chain is the exact ordered transfer product. After these operations, a tree with at most four distinguished leaves has only a fixed number of essential branching edges, while all arbitrarily long unary portions are already contained in the parity transfer product. The unique lowest common ancestor of all labels is an ordinary tree invariant. If a g derivative lands on a coarser conditional map, its mark is attached at that map and therefore moves v⊤ to that scale. Hence no marked vertex can occur above v⊤. The shell selector is applied only after the full packet at v⊤ has been collected. A remote unmarked side decoration is not cut from its parent and is not asked to carry an external Taylor factor. If exact localization turns its contribution into a smaller-hull contact, that term is already in the finite contact block and is not a shell-k packet. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(FµαFνα), δµν Tr F2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Corollary 8.40 (Vanishing rotation regulator). In the projective stress Ward identity, the antisymmetric regulator insertion is a2 times a normalized family of dimension-six roots. The marked source bounds therefore make it vanish in the zero-spacing limit. The cutoff rotation Ward identities integrate to full O(4) covariance once the already established translation, reflection, and tensor-source continuity statements are inserted. Theorem 8.46 (Euclidean covariance and Poincaré reconstruction). The Schwinger family satisfies the full O(4) covariance axiom. No unitary action of a Euclidean rotation that changes the reflection hyperplane is assumed on the intermediate OS quotient. 9 Continuum reconstruction and spectral gap 9.1 Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction and clustering gap The common Schwinger functional Let D be the countable algebra generated by positive-time translates of the bounded positive-scale cylinders and the normalized finite local source fields constructed by the marked hierarchy. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(FG) − S(F)S(G)| ≤ CF,Ge−m dist1(supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T(t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F], ∥T(t)[F] − [F]∥ 2 = S(ΘF τ2tF) − 2ℜS(ΘF τtF) + S(ΘFF), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T(t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(FµαFνα), δµν Tr F2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. The marked source bounds therefore make it vanish in the zero-spacing limit. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(FµαFνα), δµν Tr F2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Corollary 8.40 (Vanishing rotation regulator). In the projective stress Ward identity, the antisymmetric regulator insertion is a2 times a normalized family of dimension-six roots. The marked source bounds therefore make it vanish in the zero-spacing limit. The cutoff rotation Ward identities integrate to full O(4) covariance once the already established translation, reflection, and tensor-source continuity statements are inserted. The multiscale source-tree theorem supplies a projective Schwinger functional S on D with the following properties: (S1) temperedness and continuity in every Schwartz test tensor; (S2) stationarity, gauge invariance, permutation symmetry, and reflection positivity; (S3) continuous Euclidean translations; (S4) for every two field polynomials F, G with separated supports, |S(FG) − S(F)S(G)| ≤ CF,Ge−m dist1(supp F,supp G) (166) with one m > 0 independent of the chosen polynomials; (S5) the OS linear-growth estimate of Lemma 8.13 on every finite source multiplet. The constants CF,G may depend on the fixed fields and test functions; the exponent m does not. Theorem 9.1 (Continuous OS reconstruction). Let Θ be time reflection and D+ the positive-time subalgebra. The form ⟨F, G⟩OS = S(ΘF G) is positive semidefinite. Its quotient and completion give a separable Hilbert space H, vacuum Ω = [1], and a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup T(t) = e−tH , H ≥ 0. Proof. Reflection positivity gives the positive form and the null ideal N = {F : ∥F∥OS = 0}. Positive-time translations preserve D+ for sufficiently small translations on each compactly supported word and define contractions on the quotient; the usual time-zero limiting argument extends them to all t ≥ 0. For a core vector [F], ∥T(t)[F] − [F]∥ 2 = S(ΘF τ2tF) − 2ℜS(ΘF τtF) + S(ΘFF), which tends to zero by translation continuity. Contractivity and density give strong continuity on H. Reflection symmetry makes the semigroup self-adjoint, and the spectral theorem gives T(t) = e−tH with H ≥ 0. Spectral consequence of one common clustering rate Let D+,0 be the centered positive-time core, D+,0 = {F ∈ D+ : S(F) = 0}. For F ∈ D+,0 let µF be the positive spectral measure of H in the vector [F]. 89 Lemma 9.2 (Core spectral support). For every F ∈ D+,0, supp µF ⊂ [m, ∞). (167) Proof. Let the time support of F lie in a fixed compact interval. For all sufficiently large t, the supports of ΘF and τtF are separated by at least t − cF . Since S(F) = 0, (166) and OS reconstruction give 0 ≤ Z ∞ 0 e−tλ dµF (λ) = ⟨[F], T(t)[F]⟩ ≤ CF e−mt . (168) Fix ε > 0. Then e−(m−ε)t µF ([0, m − ε]) ≤ CF e−mt . Multiplication by e(m−ε)t and t → ∞ gives µF ([0, m − ε]) = 0. Letting ε ↓ 0 proves (167). Theorem 9.3 (Unique vacuum and complete local mass gap). The OS Hamiltonian satisfies H Ω⊥ ≥ m > 0. (169) The vacuum is unique. Proof. The centered classes [F] − S(F)Ω, F ∈ D+, are dense in Ω⊥ . Lemma 9.2 says that the spectral projection EH([0, m − ε]) annihilates this dense set for every ε > 0; hence it vanishes on Ω⊥ . This proves the absence of spectrum in (0, m). For a centered core vector, (168) tends to zero, so its spectral measure has no atom at zero. Density then shows that EH({0})H = CΩ. Thus the vacuum is unique and (169) holds. 10 Nontriviality and finite spectral window 10.1 Endpoint interpolation and reflected noncollapse Let Yr(f) be the tangent-normalized, Wick-centered scalar curvature source at physical scale r, with the source root parallel transported in the normalized finite-jet frame. Lemma 8.38 (No low-dimensional gauge-invariant vector). For every compact simple G there is no nonzero local, reflection-compatible, gauge-invariant vector source of engineering dimension at most four, modulo vacuum terms and total derivatives. Proof. A connection mass term is not gauge invariant. At dimension two, Tr dρ(Fµν) = 0 by semisimplicity. At dimension three, traces of dρ(DF) reduce to derivatives of Tr dρ(F) and vanish. A dimension-four gauge-invariant vector cannot be formed from two curvature two-forms using only the metric while leaving one free index; an epsilon tensor would have the wrong reflection parity. Total derivatives are excluded by the stated quotient. 86 Lemma 8.39 (Antisymmetric stress defect begins at dimension six). A local signed-hypercubic, reflection- even, gauge-invariant antisymmetric rank-two source has no component of engineering dimension four or five. Its first possible nonzero continuum jet has dimension at least six. Proof. At dimension four the quadratic curvature tensors are generated by Tr(FµαFνα), δµν Tr F2 , and the corresponding dual-curvature contractions. The first is symmetric; the dual contraction is proportional to a diagonal pseudoscalar tensor; none has an antisymmetric part. Reflection symmetry excludes the odd-derivative dimension-five sector. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF, hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). Theorem 5.18 (Compact weakening). If a > 0, a′ > 0, and a′ < a, every bounded subset of Ba,N , N ≥ 1, is relatively compact in Ba′,N−1. Proof. Let F be bounded by M in Ba,N . Theorem 5.19 (Exact fiber-chart invariance). Let Ψ1(w, z1) and Ψ2(w, z2) be two exact C1 fiber charts for the same finite-dimensional submersion B(U) = w. Suppose their images agree on the integration region and their transition map is orientation preserving. Then, for every integrable density F, Z F(Ψ1(w, z1)) J1(w, z1) dz1 = Z F(Ψ2(w, z2)) J2(w, z2) dz2. Consequently the normalized conditional expectation, its connected logarithm, and every background derivative of the complete local standard-scheme coordinate and its quadratic coefficient are independent of the chosen exact fiber chart. 48 Proof. The first identity is the ordinary change-of-variables theorem on the fiber. Division by the same fiber mass gives equality of normalized conditional expectations. Connected logarithms are functions of those expectations. Differentiation is permitted on any common dominated marked domain. The determinant statement follows because the two Jacobians are related by the determinant of the transition map, which cancels under the change of variables. It must not be inserted a second time. 5.4 Ultraviolet supplier closure The finite-volume normal chart, strict macrostep contraction, and irregular Fréchet flatness used below are not separate inputs: they are respectively Theorem 2.5, Theorem 4.30, and Theorem 3.31. Fix an engineering cutoff D. Modulo vacuum constants, total lattice differences, gauge and Bianchi identities, equation-of-motion/redundant directions, and the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills coordinate, the local gauge-invariant curvature jets of dimension at most D form a finite graded space J≤D = M ∆≤D J∆. The same remains true after adjoining any fixed finite collection of retained, source, displacement, profile, stress, rotation-defect, and one/two-root marks. Proof. After a boundary-rooted tree gauge, one enlarged block cell contains a finite alphabet of Lie-algebra variables and difference labels. Jets of bounded engineering dimension form a finite polynomial span. Every listed quotient relation is linear on that span, and adjoining finitely many marks gives a finite direct sum. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF, hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). Theorem 5.18 (Compact weakening). If a > 0, a′ > 0, and a′ < a, every bounded subset of Ba,N , N ≥ 1, is relatively compact in Ba′,N−1. Proof. Let F be bounded by M in Ba,N . For a cutoff L, sup e X X∋e |X|>L ea′ |X| ∥FX∥CN−1 ≤ e−(a−a′ )L M, uniformly in F ∈ F. For |X| ≤ L, only finitely many rooted support shapes occur. On each shape, the CN (KX) bound is uniform, and the compact embedding CN (KX) ⋐ CN−1 (KX) follows from Arzela–Ascoli in finitely many coordinate charts. A diagonal subsequence converges on all shapes of size at most L. Letting L increase and using the uniform tail estimate proves relative compactness in Ba′,N−1. Theorem 5.19 (Exact fiber-chart invariance). Let Ψ1(w, z1) and Ψ2(w, z2) be two exact C1 fiber charts for the same finite-dimensional submersion B(U) = w. Suppose their images agree on the integration region and their transition map is orientation preserving. Then, for every integrable density F, Z F(Ψ1(w, z1)) J1(w, z1) dz1 = Z F(Ψ2(w, z2)) J2(w, z2) dz2. Consequently the normalized conditional expectation, its connected logarithm, and every background derivative of the complete local standard-scheme coordinate and its quadratic coefficient are independent of the chosen exact fiber chart. 48 Proof. The first identity is the ordinary change-of-variables theorem on the fiber. Division by the same fiber mass gives equality of normalized conditional expectations. Connected logarithms are functions of those expectations. Differentiation is permitted on any common dominated marked domain. The determinant statement follows because the two Jacobians are related by the determinant of the transition map, which cancels under the change of variables. It must not be inserted a second time. 5.4 Ultraviolet supplier closure The finite-volume normal chart, strict macrostep contraction, and irregular Fréchet flatness used below are not separate inputs: they are respectively Theorem 2.5, Theorem 4.30, and Theorem 3.31. Theorem 5.18 (Compact weakening). If a > 0, a′ > 0, and a′ < a, every bounded subset of Ba,N , N ≥ 1, is relatively compact in Ba′,N−1. Proof. Let F be bounded by M in Ba,N . Fix an engineering cutoff D. Modulo vacuum constants, total lattice differences, gauge and Bianchi identities, equation-of-motion/redundant directions, and the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills coordinate, the local gauge-invariant curvature jets of dimension at most D form a finite graded space J≤D = M ∆≤D J∆. The same remains true after adjoining any fixed finite collection of retained, source, displacement, profile, stress, rotation-defect, and one/two-root marks. Proof. After a boundary-rooted tree gauge, one enlarged block cell contains a finite alphabet of Lie-algebra variables and difference labels. Jets of bounded engineering dimension form a finite polynomial span. Every listed quotient relation is linear on that span, and adjoining finitely many marks gives a finite direct sum. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF, hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The next possible rank-two complement after dimension four therefore begins at dimension six. 49 Proposition 5.24 (Finite-order marked RG bridge to the associated-graded block). The maps include the regular/irregular partition of unity before the logarithm is taken, so no all-good denominator occurs. Write Wm(J) = log Zm(J) − log Zm(0) for the normalized finite-volume source logarithm. Iterating the exact maps Rm, . . . , Rjw and then the finite macrobridge is an identity, not an asymptotic expansion. A scale-labelled source forest is generated recursively as follows. A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Terms transported without joining retain their existing components. At the terminal matching logarithm, the remaining components are joined by the matching-scale connected cumulants. The ordering of children is fixed by the least source label, so isomorphic terms are not counted more than once. Lemma 8.6 (Exact multiscale Faà di Bruno forest formula). Each analytic coefficient of each exact conditional logarithm occurs exactly once. After absolute values are taken, the sum is dominated uniformly in m by the rooted weak rows and the finite matching expansion. Hence (115) passes to the infinite weak-depth limit termwise for every fixed n. Proof. For one conditional integration, differentiation of the normalized logarithm is the joint-cumulant identity. The set-partition formula for a derivative of a composition is precisely the Banach-valued Faà di Bruno formula: every block of the partition is one incoming connected component and the outer cumulant joins those blocks at the current scale. Fixing the least-label order makes this representation unique. Induction over the finite sequence of exact conditional integrations proves (115); the terminal matching logarithm is the final induction step. Lemma 5.22 (No reflection-even scalar of engineering dimension five). In four-dimensional pure fixed-G lattice gauge theory, the signed-hypercubic and reflection-even gauge-invariant scalar jet quotient has no engineering-dimension-five component. Proof. A nonvacuum dimension-five scalar would have to contain two curvature factors and one covariant difference, hence five coordinate indices before contraction. The invariant tensors of the signed hypercubic group are generated by even-rank Kronecker contractions and the rank-four alternating tensor. They cannot contract an odd total of five indices to a scalar without a preferred vector. Total differences and Bianchi descendants are already removed in the quotient. Thus the reflection-even scalar sector jumps from the extracted dimension-four Yang–Mills density to dimension at least six. Lemma 5.23 (No reflection-even rank-two curvature jet of dimension five). In the local gauge-invariant rank-two curvature-jet quotient relevant to the stress/displacement source, the reflection-even engineering- dimension-five component is zero. Proof. A dimension-five curvature bilinear has the schematic Lorentz-index content F DF, hence five tensor indices before contractions. To leave exactly two free rank-two indices one would have to contract an odd set of three indices. The signed-hypercubic invariant tensors available in the reflection-even sector are products of Kronecker deltas and pairs of Levi–Civita tensors, all of even rank. A single Levi–Civita tensor is reflection odd. Thus no reflection-even constant coefficient tensor can perform the required contraction. Terms in which the derivative is moved onto the whole bilinear are total differences, while Bianchi and equation-of-motion descendants are already quotiented. The maps include the regular/irregular partition of unity before the logarithm is taken, so no all-good denominator occurs. Write Wm(J) = log Zm(J) − log Zm(0) for the normalized finite-volume source logarithm. Iterating the exact maps Rm, . . . , Rjw and then the finite macrobridge is an identity, not an asymptotic expansion. A scale-labelled source forest is generated recursively as follows. A source derivative is a labelled leaf. At one conditional integration, connected cumulant differentiation joins a nonempty partition of the incoming leaves and decorated subtrees to one new vertex labelled by that integration scale. Terms transported without joining retain their existing components. At the terminal matching logarithm, the remaining components are joined by the matching-scale connected cumulants. The ordering of children is fixed by the least source label, so isomorphic terms are not counted more than once. Lemma 8.6 (Exact multiscale Faà di Bruno forest formula). For every finite depth m and every fixed derivative order n, Dn Wm(0)[J1, . . . , Jn] = X τ∈Tm,n Am(τ; J1, . . . , Jn), (115) where Tm,n is the finite family of recursively generated scale-labelled connected trees described above. Each analytic coefficient of each exact conditional logarithm occurs exactly once. After absolute values are taken, the sum is dominated uniformly in m by the rooted weak rows and the finite matching expansion. Hence (115) passes to the infinite weak-depth limit termwise for every fixed n. Proof. For one conditional integration, differentiation of the normalized logarithm is the joint-cumulant identity. The set-partition formula for a derivative of a composition is precisely the Banach-valued Faà di Bruno formula: every block of the partition is one incoming connected component and the outer cumulant joins those blocks at the current scale. Fixing the least-label order makes this representation unique. Induction over the finite sequence of exact conditional integrations proves (115); the terminal matching logarithm is the final induction step. The weak rooted margin pays every nonroot weak vertex by σ < 1, while the finite macrobridge and matching KP expansion pay the finitely many terminal vertices. The one/two-root bounds control a component while its source leaves remain external. These majorants are summable independently of m, so dominated convergence gives the last assertion. For every fixed compact connected simple G and faithful unitary representation ρ, the group register CG is finite and all hypotheses consumed by Sections 2–10 are satisfied. Consequently Theorem 1.1 holds. Proof. Compactness and the analytic bi-invariant geometry give the Karcher, logarithm, coarea, and faithful-action constants of Section 2. The complete folded block symbol is spacetime-only and tensors with Ig, so the strict right-inverse and optical coercivity constants are unchanged. The chart complement is charged by the faithful Wilson action and the irregular activity is exponentially small. The permanent weak map, centered graph, and BPHZL packet use the same finite-dimensional Lie-algebra tensor calculus, with the universal color factor CA(G). The Peter–Weyl spectral sum converges at the fixed order sG, and the higher hybrid-polydisc argument supplies the one-pivot nuclear and multipivot Fourier–Wiener rows. The ordinary-periodic toron, seam, reflection, and wrapping templates are admitted by Theorem D.3; no twisted sector or finite-volume bundle sum is used. The invariant-jet theorem supplies the complete low-dimensional mixing and dimension-six regulator spaces. The joint Haar–optical forest, source transport, Ward hierarchy, OS reconstruction, and noncollapse theorem then apply with constants depending on G but uniform in cutoff, volume, and directed depth. Appendix F, specifically Table 3, records every independent entry of CG, the first proof call at which its G-dependence enters, and the subsequent consumers. Thus no additional estimate uniform in G is hidden in this completion step: after those finite calls, each remaining mechanism is color-free, tensors with Ig, or takes a finite maximum in a registered finite-dimensional space. Let C (L) r be the zero-mode-removed transverse covariance remaining after the weak flow is stopped at scale r on a periodic torus of side L ≥ 4r. For every complete packet class λ, the one-open-leg coefficient vanishes by global color invariance.
